summary: Steven Willmott, CEO of Safe Intelligence, presents the case for spec-driven validation of AI agents. His company has spent three years applying formal verification techniques to ML models—originally vision and tabular models—examining entire regions of input space for perturbation-induced failures. They have now released a product that does analogous testing for language models by generating edge cases and test cases. The central thesis is that a smarter agent is not automatically a better or safer agent. Using the Hitchhiker's Guide character Marvin as a metaphor, Willmott illustrates that massive capability brings problems: jailbreaks like wrapping malicious instructions in poems work better on large models because they understand the poem and execute the hidden instruction, while small models simply fail to comprehend it. Broader-remint agents create more exploitable surface area and infrastructure access. There is also a cost dimension—using large models for simple tasks wastes tokens and adds latency. The ideal is a model good enough to perform its task but not capable of arbitrary harm. Spec-driven validation means defining what an agent should do independent of its implementation. Components include: ground-truth datasets, explicit rules (e.g., never exceed 10% discount), domain ontologies and dictionaries (e.g., an airline's actual destinations), internal company terminology, domain knowledge about substitutable terms, rights and roles, and robustness requirements (tolerance for typos, rephrasing, input variation). This goes beyond the eval test set toward integration-test-style benchmarks. Such specs can drive security testing—since agents are most vulnerable in the domains they are designed to operate in—and robustness testing by varying inputs to measure stability. Willmott emphasizes that specs must stay independent of implementation platforms like LangSmith or Vertex agents so that integration tests, unit tests, and penetration tests survive infrastructure changes. This independence enables closing the loop: running the agent automatically, analyzing results, and iterating to fill robustness gaps—a process he describes as 'backyard RL,' not proper RL but jury-rigged iteration around the model. Drawing on his experience co-authoring the OpenAPI spec, Willmott envisions agent specs as open, version-controlled artifacts in GitHub repos that can be pulled into any tool. Creating variations within the boundaries a spec defines remains hard, but the key message is to capture task and context, not just eval benchmarks.

takeaways: Larger models are not straightforwardly safer: poem-based jailbreaks succeed against large models but fail against small ones that cannot understand the poem.
Broader agent capabilities create more attack surface and more infrastructure access to abuse, creating a smart-vs-safe trade-off.
An agent spec must go beyond a test dataset to include explicit rules, domain ontologies, internal terminology, rights/roles, and robustness requirements.
Specs should be written independently of the implementation so they survive a model or infrastructure swap and can drive security and robustness testing.
Implementation-independent specs enable closing the loop: automated agent runs, result analysis, and iteration to fill robustness gaps—a 'backyard RL' approach.
Willmott envisions open, version-controlled agent specs analogous to the OpenAPI spec, stored in GitHub repos and portable across tools.
Agents are most vulnerable in the domains they are designed to operate in, making spec-defined boundaries natural targets for security testing.
Robustness requirements—tolerance for typos, rephrasing, and input variation—are essential and analogous to perturbation testing in vision models.
Creating input variations within the envelope a spec defines remains technically hard, but capturing task and context alongside eval data is the essential starting point.

sections.title: Introduction and Company Background
sections.summary: Willmott introduces himself as CEO of Safe Intelligence, a 3-year-old company specializing in ML validation using formal verification techniques, originally for vision and tabular models. They released a new product for LLM testing via edge-case generation. He references the company booth and branded ducks.

sections.title: Spec-Driven Validation Motivation: Smarter Is Not Always Better
sections.summary: Willmott frames the core problem: the assumption that a smarter agent is a better agent is flawed. He uses Marvin from Hitchhiker's Guide as a metaphor. Jailbreaks like poem-encapsulated malicious instructions work better on large models because they understand and execute them, while small models do not. Broader agent remit means more attack surface. Cost and latency are also concerns. The goal is a model good enough to perform but not capable of arbitrary harm.

sections.title: Components of an Agent Specification
sections.summary: Willmott details what goes beyond a test dataset: explicit rules (e.g., max 10% discount), domain ontologies (airline destinations), internal company terminology, domain knowledge about substitutable terms (gross profit vs. gross sales), rights and roles, and robustness requirements (typos, rephrasing, input variation). He emphasizes going beyond the eval to integration-test-style benchmarks and mentions agent cards from the A2A spec as useful but insufficient.

sections.title: Using Specs for Security and Robustness Testing
sections.summary: Safe Intelligence's platform uses agent specs for two purposes: security checks (agents are most vulnerable in domains they operate in) and robustness testing (varying inputs to measure answer stability). Willmott notes the point is not to promote the product but to encourage explicit spec construction. He references prompt management platforms and agent cards, noting that even with agent cards, additional range and robustness specifications are needed for full evaluation.

sections.title: Implementation Independence, Closing the Loop, and Open Spec Vision
sections.summary: Willmott stresses that agent specs must stay independent of implementation platforms like LangSmith or Vertex agents so that integration tests, unit tests, and penetration tests survive infrastructure changes. This independence enables closing the loop—running agents automatically, analyzing results, and iterating to fill robustness gaps, which he calls 'backyard RL.' Drawing on his experience co-authoring the OpenAPI spec, he envisions open, version-controlled agent specs in GitHub repos portable across tools. He invites collaboration and promotes the company booth's LEGO prize game.

demonstrations: Safe Intelligence released a new product for LLM edge-case and test-case generation, announced the day before the talk.
Safe Intelligence applies formal verification techniques to vision and tabular models, examining whole regions of input space for perturbation failures.
limitations: For LLMs, Safe Intelligence does not have access to the model itself, so it relies on clever test-case generation rather than formal verification of input regions.
Agent cards from the A2A spec are insufficient on their own for full agent evaluation without supplemental robustness and range specifications.
Testing that a rule is never violated is inherently difficult.
Creating variations within the envelope a spec creates remains technically hard.
quantitativeClaims: Safe Intelligence has been around for 3 years.
Example rule: never offer more than 10% discount.
Example rule: no refunds more than 30 days past purchase.

evidence.excerpt: if you encapsulate something in a poem and you give that to a relatively low-end model, the low-end model doesn't even understand the poem. Whereas a larger model will be like, Oh, I can take this out and I can execute the bad instruction that's wrapped up in the poem.
evidence.supports: Poem-based jailbreaks succeed against large models but fail against small ones, showing bigger is not safer.

evidence.excerpt: don't ever give a discount more than 10%. Uh we don't allow refunds if um if you know, it's more than 30 days past the purchase
evidence.supports: Agent specs must include explicit business rules with concrete thresholds.

evidence.excerpt: could typos disrupt it? How many typos disrupt it? Like how frustrated will people get? Rephrasing, how how stable under change are are the results?
evidence.supports: Robustness requirements include tolerance for typos and rephrasing, analogous to perturbation testing in vision models.

evidence.excerpt: if you know what an agent is trying to do, you know the edges of where it's vulnerable because it's going to be willing to talk about those domains that it's supposed to act in
evidence.supports: Agent specs inform security testing because agents are most vulnerable in their operational domains.

evidence.excerpt: Stay independent of the implementation cuz often you may, you know, may you may be building in LangSmith or something uh or Vertex agents or or so on, but then later on you may change to a different infrastructure. You actually want to keep those integration tests, all of the unit tests, and penetration tests and and run them independently.
evidence.supports: Specs must be implementation-independent so tests survive infrastructure changes.

evidence.excerpt: part of our inspiration of thinking about what should go into a spec is like, what would you need uh to actually run the agent automatically, get the results, and then start to iterate and try to fill the robustness gaps that have appeared. So, it's like a backyard type of RL
evidence.supports: Specs enable closing the loop of automated agent runs and iterative robustness improvement, described as backyard RL.

evidence.excerpt: I helped write that spec way back in the day. Uh so, all about open. So, we're thinking about like, how do you express these things in a way that you could just have in a GitHub repo, pull them into whatever tool you want
evidence.supports: Willmott envisions open, version-controlled agent specs analogous to the OpenAPI spec, portable across tools.
